stem: A team wants coding conventions to be shared with everyone who clones the repository and applied automatically in every session. Where should these conventions live?

options.A: In project-level CLAUDE.md (root or .claude/CLAUDE.md), committed to the repo
options.B: In each developer's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, kept in sync by hand
options.C: Pasted into the system prompt at the start of every session by each developer
options.D: In a .claude/skills/ skill that each developer invokes manually when needed

explanation: Project-level CLAUDE.md (root CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md) is committed to version control, so it is shared with the whole team and always loaded into context. This is the canonical place for shared, always-on conventions.

distractors.B: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and NOT shared via version control, so teammates would not get the conventions.
distractors.C: Manually pasting into the system prompt is not shared, not version-controlled, and error-prone.
distractors.D: Skills require on-demand manual invocation; they are not always loaded, so conventions would be applied inconsistently.

stem: A developer wants to keep a few personal Claude Code preferences (preferred commit message style, verbosity) that should NOT affect teammates. Where should these go?

options.A: A directory-level CLAUDE.md in the repo's src/ folder, committed with the code
options.B: A .claude/rules/ file with a broad glob pattern so it matches most edits
options.C: The root CLAUDE.md, committed to the repo alongside the team's conventions
options.D: The user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md in the developer's home directory

explanation: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal preferences that apply across all of a developer's projects and are never shared via version control, making it the correct home for individual, non-team settings.

distractors.A: A directory CLAUDE.md inside the repo is still committed and shared with teammates.
distractors.B: A .claude/rules/ file in the repo is shared and scoped by file path, not by individual user.
distractors.C: Root CLAUDE.md is committed and shared, so personal preferences would leak to the whole team.

stem: Your CI job runs `claude "Review this diff for security issues"` and the build hangs until it times out. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Set a shorter session timeout in the CI configuration so the job exits sooner
options.B: Wrap the command so it pipes 'yes' into Claude Code's stdin to answer prompts
options.C: Add the --interactive=false flag so the CLI skips the interactive session
options.D: Add the -p (print) flag: claude -p "Review this diff for security issues"

explanation: The -p (or --print) flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, writes output to stdout, and exits. Without it, Claude Code waits for interactive input and hangs in CI.

distractors.A: A shorter timeout just makes the job fail faster; it does not make Claude Code run non-interactively.
distractors.B: Piping 'yes' into stdin is a fragile hack that does not properly invoke non-interactive mode.
distractors.C: --interactive=false is not a real Claude Code flag; -p is the supported mechanism.

stem: Which statement best captures the difference between CLAUDE.md and a skill?

options.A: CLAUDE.md defines the tools Claude is allowed to call; skills carry the project docs
options.B: The two are interchangeable; which one you put guidance in is purely a stylistic choice
options.C: Skills are always loaded; CLAUDE.md is loaded only when a file matching its scope is edited
options.D: CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded universal standards; skills are invoked on demand per workflow

explanation: CLAUDE.md is always loaded into context and carries universal, always-on standards. Skills are invoked on demand for specific task workflows, keeping their (often verbose) instructions out of context until needed.

distractors.A: Neither is primarily a tool-definition mechanism; both carry instructions/workflows, not tool schemas.
distractors.B: They serve distinct purposes (always-on vs on-demand), so the choice is functional, not stylistic.
distractors.C: This reverses the truth: CLAUDE.md is always loaded; skills are on-demand.

stem: Claude Code is behaving inconsistently across sessions and you suspect a stale or wrong memory file is being loaded. Which command helps you verify which memory (CLAUDE.md) files are active?

options.A: `/config` — expecting it to print the configuration and memory files in effect
options.B: `/rules` — expecting it to list the instruction files loaded for this session
options.C: `/reload` — expecting it to re-read and report the memory files it picks up
options.D: `/memory` — expecting it to list the memory files currently loaded

explanation: The /memory command reports which memory (CLAUDE.md) files are currently loaded and at which scope, letting you diagnose hierarchy issues such as a user-level file conflicting with project-level instructions. The other three options name commands that do not report loaded memory files, so none of them answers the diagnostic question.

distractors.A: /config surfaces configuration settings, not the set of memory files loaded and the scope each came from — it cannot tell you that a user-level CLAUDE.md is shadowing a project one.
distractors.B: /rules is not a Claude Code command; nothing lists loaded CLAUDE.md memory files under that name.
distractors.C: /reload is not a Claude Code diagnostic. Even a reload would only re-read files, not report which ones are in effect.

stem: Your repo has Terraform under infrastructure/, React components under web/, and Python services under services/. Test files live next to the source files they cover throughout all three trees. You want testing conventions to apply to every test file regardless of location, while each language tree keeps its own conventions. What is the best configuration?

options.A: Put the testing conventions in a directory CLAUDE.md at the repo root, above all three trees
options.B: Create a testing-conventions skill that developers invoke before writing any test file
options.C: Put all conventions, testing included, in one large root CLAUDE.md loaded for every file
options.D: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files in each language tree, plus a .claude/rules/ file globbing "**/*.test.*"

explanation: Directory CLAUDE.md files are ideal when conventions are contained within a single directory tree (the per-language conventions). Path-specific .claude/rules/ with glob patterns are ideal when conventions must apply to files spread across the codebase by type (test files everywhere). Combining them matches each need.

distractors.A: A directory CLAUDE.md at the root applies to the whole tree, not selectively to test files by type.
distractors.B: A manually invoked skill is not reliable for always-on conventions and adds friction.
distractors.C: A single root CLAUDE.md loads everything for every file, wasting context and mixing unrelated conventions.

stem: You want a custom slash command that accepts a free-form argument the user types after the command name (e.g., /triage <issue-url>) and injects it into the prompt. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Reference the $ARGUMENTS placeholder in the command's markdown body
options.B: Add context: fork to the command frontmatter so the argument runs in its own context
options.C: Define a JSON schema in the command file describing the shape of the argument
options.D: Add an argument-hint frontmatter key and let Claude parse the value the user typed

explanation: Custom slash commands substitute the text the user supplies into the command body via the $ARGUMENTS placeholder. This is the mechanism for passing free-form input to a command.

distractors.B: context: fork controls isolated execution context; it does not capture command arguments.
distractors.C: Commands do not take a JSON argument schema; $ARGUMENTS is the substitution mechanism.
distractors.D: argument-hint is a skill frontmatter affordance that prompts for parameters; it is not how commands receive substituted argument text.

stem: You are authoring a codebase-analysis skill that produces hundreds of lines of exploratory output. You want that output kept out of the main conversation so it does not consume the user's context budget. Which frontmatter setting accomplishes this?

options.A: `output: summary`, to have the skill return only a condensed summary of its work
options.B: `context: fork`, to run the skill in an isolated execution context
options.C: `allowed-tools: [Read, Grep, Glob]`, to limit the skill to read-only tools
options.D: `argument-hint: "target directory"`, to prompt for the directory to analyse

explanation: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its verbose output does not pollute the main conversation; only a summary returns. This is the recommended pattern for verbose/exploratory skills.

distractors.A: output: summary is not a real frontmatter key, so the skill would run unchanged and its full output would land in the main conversation.
distractors.C: allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill may call. That bounds what it can do, not where its output goes.
distractors.D: argument-hint prompts for a parameter at invocation time; it has no bearing on context isolation.

stem: A skill is supposed to operate read-only (it should never modify files), but it occasionally writes files when the model decides to. What is the most reliable way to guarantee it cannot write?

options.A: Set context: fork so any writes happen in an isolated context rather than the repo
options.B: Set allowed-tools to a read-only set such as Read, Grep and Glob
options.C: Add a sentence to the skill body instructing it never to modify any files
options.D: Add an argument-hint warning the user that the skill is meant to be read-only

explanation: (B) is the only deterministic control. allowed-tools restricts the tools available during skill execution, so limiting it to a read-only set makes the write and edit tools simply unavailable rather than relying on the model to comply with prose.

distractors.A: context: fork isolates the skill's context, but a forked context still has the write tools and can still modify files.
distractors.C: A prose instruction is probabilistic — the same failure mode the stem already describes, since the model is choosing to write despite intent.
distractors.D: argument-hint only prompts for a parameter; a warning aimed at the user restricts nothing about what the skill may call.

stem: Two files in `.claude/rules/` match the file you are editing: `general.md` with `paths: ["src/**/*"]` and `payments.md` with `paths: ["src/payments/**/*.ts"]`. You are editing `src/payments/charge.ts`. What actually happens?

options.A: Only the more specific glob loads; the narrower pattern overrides the broader one.
options.B: Both files load and concatenate; there is no documented override, so conflicts resolve arbitrarily.
options.C: Neither loads; Claude skips conflicting path rules and falls back to `CLAUDE.md`.
options.D: The first glob to match loads and later matches are ignored.

explanation: Path-scoped rules follow the same concatenate-don't-override model as CLAUDE.md files: every rule whose glob matches the file being read is loaded into context, and the documentation describes no priority system between them. If two matching rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily, so consistency across rules is the author's responsibility. The one ordering rule that does exist is between scopes, not globs — user-level rules load before project rules, which gives project rules the later (more salient) position.

distractors.A: Specificity controls *when* a rule loads, not which rule wins. A narrower glob simply matches fewer files; it does not suppress a broader rule that also matches.
distractors.C: Matching rules are always applied, never discarded. There is no conflict-detection step that skips them.
distractors.D: There is no first-match-wins behaviour — every matching rule loads.

stem: You want to keep your monolithic root CLAUDE.md from growing unwieldy. Standards for API conventions, testing, and deployment each live in their own markdown files under standards/. What is the recommended way to compose them into CLAUDE.md?

options.A: Convert each standards file into a separate skill and invoke them all at session start
options.B: Use @import references such as @import ./standards/api-conventions.md from CLAUDE.md
options.C: Move all the standards into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so they load globally for every project
options.D: Copy the full text of each standards file into CLAUDE.md and keep the copies in sync by hand

explanation: @import lets CLAUDE.md reference external files, keeping it modular. Each package's CLAUDE.md can import only the standards relevant to its domain, avoiding a giant monolith and avoiding manual duplication.

distractors.A: Skills are on-demand and would not reliably load always-on standards at every session.
distractors.C: User-level CLAUDE.md is not shared with the team and is not the modularization mechanism.
distractors.D: Copying and manually syncing duplicates content and drifts out of date.

stem: Your CI generates unit tests, but many duplicate tests that already exist or cover trivial getters/setters. What two-part change most improves generated test quality?

options.A: Run the generator twice on each file and keep only the tests that appear in both runs
options.B: Lower temperature to 0 and raise max_tokens so the generator produces tighter output
options.C: Supply the existing test files as context and document testing standards and valuable-test criteria in CLAUDE.md
options.D: Only run test generation on the files whose measured code coverage is below target

explanation: Supplying existing test files lets the generator avoid duplicating scenarios, and documenting testing standards and what counts as a valuable test in CLAUDE.md steers it away from trivial getters/setters. Both address the underlying knowledge gap.

distractors.A: Running twice does not give the model knowledge of existing tests or quality criteria.
distractors.B: Temperature and token limits do not tell the model what tests already exist or which are worth writing.
distractors.D: Coverage targeting helps prioritize but still produces duplicates and trivial tests without the missing context.

stem: You want to guarantee that whenever Claude Code edits a file under src/, the formatter runs and the file is reformatted before the change is considered done, without relying on the model to remember. Which hook fits best?

options.A: A Stop hook that returns additionalContext reminding Claude to format what it edited
options.B: A line in CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to always run the formatter after editing
options.C: A PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter on the edited file
options.D: A PreToolUse hook that blocks any edit to a file under src/ before it is written

explanation: (C) is the right hook stage: PostToolUse fires after a tool has run, which is exactly when the just-written file exists on disk and can be reformatted. That makes the format step deterministic instead of depending on the model remembering to run it.

distractors.A: A Stop hook fires when the turn ends and additionalContext only nudges the model, so formatting stays probabilistic — the stem asks for a guarantee.
distractors.B: A CLAUDE.md instruction is probabilistic; the model may skip formatting, which is exactly the dependency the stem wants removed.
distractors.D: PreToolUse fires before the write, so there is no file to format yet; blocking edits to src/ stops the work rather than formatting it.

stem: Company policy forbids editing files under config/secrets/. Developers occasionally still ask Claude Code to touch them. What gives the strongest, deterministic guarantee that such edits are blocked before they happen?

options.A: A PreToolUse hook that inspects the target path and denies Edit/Write under config/secrets/
options.B: Few-shot examples in the prompt showing Claude refusing to edit config/secrets/
options.C: A PostToolUse hook that reverts any change made under config/secrets/ right after the write
options.D: A bold warning in CLAUDE.md telling Claude it must never edit files under config/secrets/

explanation: PreToolUse hooks intercept a tool call before it executes and can deterministically deny it based on the target path. This blocks the edit before any change is made, which prompt-based approaches cannot guarantee.

distractors.B: Few-shot examples reduce but do not eliminate the failure rate; they are not deterministic.
distractors.C: A PostToolUse revert lets the write happen first (briefly exposing secrets) and is reactive, not preventive.
distractors.D: A CLAUDE.md warning is probabilistic and can be ignored by the model.

stem: You want a workflow where, when Claude tries to end its turn, a Stop hook checks whether the test suite passed; if not, it should feed the failing test output back to Claude and let it keep working in the SAME turn, without the hook being treated as an error. In Claude Code v2.1.163+, what is the correct hook output?

options.A: Return a PreToolUse deny decision so the turn is blocked before Claude stops
options.B: Return hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext containing the failing test output
options.C: Write the failures into CLAUDE.md so they are loaded at the start of the next session
options.D: Exit with a non-zero status code and print the failing test output to stderr

explanation: As of v2.1.163 (June 2026), Stop and SubagentStop hooks can return hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (B) to feed Claude context and continue the SAME turn without the hook being treated as an error. The additionalContext payload is capped at 10,000 characters, so the hook should truncate long test output before returning it.

distractors.A: PreToolUse is the wrong hook stage entirely — it gates tool calls before they run and has no bearing on what happens when Claude tries to end a turn.
distractors.C: Writing to CLAUDE.md affects a future session's context. The stem asks for continuation within the SAME turn.
distractors.D: A non-zero exit is treated as a hook error, which is precisely the outcome the stem rules out, and stderr text is not fed back as usable context.

stem: You are packaging your team's set of skills as a Claude Code plugin so a colleague can use them. Using the May 2026 workflow, you run `claude plugin init mytools` and place SKILL.md files in the plugin's .claude/skills directories. What is the result for the colleague?

options.A: The skills auto-load as mytools@skills-dir with no marketplace or install step
options.B: The skills must be published to a marketplace and installed before they are usable
options.C: The skills only work if added to the colleague's user-level CLAUDE.md
options.D: The colleague must copy each SKILL.md into their own ~/.claude/skills manually

explanation: As of May 2026, `claude plugin init <name>` scaffolds a plugin, and skills placed in its .claude/skills directories auto-load as <name>@skills-dir with no marketplace publish or install step required.

distractors.B: The whole point of the May 2026 change is that no marketplace or install step is needed.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md is for instructions, not for registering plugin skills; auto-load handles registration.
distractors.D: Manual copying into ~/.claude/skills is the old, friction-heavy approach this feature removes.

stem: Your single Claude Code session writes a feature and then reviews its own diff, but it consistently rates its own code as fine and misses real bugs. What is the most effective architectural change?

options.A: Run the review in a separate reviewer subagent with an isolated context
options.B: Increase the model's temperature so the review explores more varied criticisms
options.C: Re-run the same session twice and merge the two reviews into one findings list
options.D: Tell the same session in the prompt to act as a harsh, skeptical reviewer

explanation: A session that generated code is less effective at critically reviewing its own changes because it shares the implementer's assumptions and context. Using a separate reviewer subagent with isolated context removes that bias and catches more real issues.

distractors.B: Temperature changes randomness, not the structural self-review bias.
distractors.C: Re-running the same context inherits the same blind spots both times.
distractors.D: Prompting the same biased context to be 'harsh' does not remove the shared assumptions that cause blind spots.

stem: Your automated PR review runs on every push. After a developer addresses the first round and pushes again, the second run re-flags the already-fixed issues and adds new ones, spamming the PR with duplicate comments. What is the best fix?

options.A: Include the prior review findings in context and report only new or still-unaddressed issues
options.B: Only review the files changed in the latest commit, ignoring the earlier ones
options.C: Clear all context before each run so every review starts from a clean slate
options.D: Post the full review on every push and let developers ignore the duplicates

explanation: Incremental reviews should carry prior findings into context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. This prevents duplicate comments while still catching newly introduced problems.

distractors.B: Reviewing only latest-commit files misses cross-file integration issues introduced by the changes.
distractors.C: Clearing context guarantees the same issues get re-flagged because the model has no memory of prior findings.
distractors.D: Spamming duplicates and relying on developers to filter degrades trust in the tool.

stem: A shared project skill named /deploy works well for the team, but you personally want a slightly different variant that does an extra dry-run step, without changing the team's behavior or affecting teammates. What is the cleanest approach?

options.A: Add context: fork to the project skill so it runs differently in your sessions
options.B: Override the team skill by defining deploy in your ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
options.C: Edit the project's .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md and keep the edit uncommitted locally
options.D: Create a differently named variant under ~/.claude/skills/, such as deploy-dryrun

explanation: Personal skill customization is done by creating a variant in user-level ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name. This is private, does not touch the shared project skill, and avoids affecting teammates.

distractors.A: context: fork changes context isolation, not the deploy steps, and editing the shared skill affects everyone.
distractors.B: CLAUDE.md cannot redefine a skill's steps; it is not the skill mechanism.
distractors.C: Editing the committed project skill risks affecting teammates and creates messy 'do not commit' state.

stem: Your team wants every member to share a GitHub MCP server when they open the repo in Claude Code, but each member's personal access token must NOT be committed. What is the correct configuration?

options.A: Commit the token into .mcp.json so the server works immediately on clone
options.B: Add the server to each developer's user-level config and have everyone replicate it
options.C: Add the server to project-scoped .mcp.json and reference the token as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}
options.D: Add the server configuration to the project CLAUDE.md with the token inline

explanation: (C) combines the two things the requirement needs. Project-scoped .mcp.json is committed to version control, so the server is available to everyone on clone; ${VAR} environment-variable expansion resolves the token at launch from each developer's own environment, so no secret is committed. Each developer sets GITHUB_TOKEN locally.

distractors.A: Committing the token makes the server work on clone, but it leaks a live credential into version control — the one thing the stem forbids.
distractors.B: User-level config is not shared, so every member has to replicate it by hand and the setup drifts; the goal was that it just works on clone.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.md carries instructions, not MCP server definitions, so the server would not register — and the inline token still commits a secret.

stem: You need a custom `/review` slash command for your team's standard code-review workflow, and it must be available to every teammate who clones the repository. Where should you create the command file?

options.A: In a Markdown file under `.claude/commands/` in the project repository
options.B: In a Markdown file under `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory
options.C: As a section of the repository's root `CLAUDE.md`, alongside the conventions
options.D: As an entry in `.claude/config.json` at the root of the project repository

explanation: Project commands stored in `.claude/commands/` are version-controlled with the repository and automatically available to everyone who clones it — exactly the requirement for a shared team command.

distractors.B: `~/.claude/commands/` holds personal commands on one developer's machine; teammates would not get the command from a clone.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md carries instructions and context, not slash-command definitions.
distractors.D: `.claude/config.json` is not a mechanism for defining slash commands.

stem: You need to restructure a monolithic application into microservices — a change spanning dozens of files and requiring service-boundary decisions. What approach should you use in Claude Code?

options.A: Use planning mode first to explore the codebase and design the approach before making any edits
options.B: Use direct execution and refactor incrementally, extracting one piece of the monolith at a time
options.C: Use direct execution with very detailed up-front instructions describing the target architecture
options.D: Start with direct execution and switch to planning mode only when the work becomes difficult

explanation: Planning mode is designed exactly for large changes with multiple possible approaches and architectural decisions. Exploring the codebase and designing the decomposition before editing avoids committing to a flawed structure across dozens of files.

distractors.B: Incremental direct execution without an up-front design risks expensive rework when early service-boundary choices prove wrong.
distractors.C: Detailed up-front instructions assume you already know the right structure, which is precisely what needs to be discovered through exploration.
distractors.D: Switching to planning only after problems appear is reactive; by then poor architectural choices may already be baked into the changes.

stem: Your CI pipeline runs the Claude Code CLI in `--print` mode with CLAUDE.md providing project context for code review, and developers find the reviews substantive. However, integrating findings is painful: Claude outputs narrative paragraphs that must be manually copied into PR comments. The team wants to automatically post each finding as a separate inline PR comment at the relevant place in code, which requires structured data with file path, line number, severity level, and suggested fix. Which approach is most effective?

options.A: Add an "Output Format for Review" section to CLAUDE.md with examples of structured findings to follow
options.B: Use the CLI flags `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, then parse the result and post inline comments via the GitHub API
options.C: Require each finding in the review prompt to follow a parseable template such as `[FILE:path] [LINE:n] [SEVERITY:level]`
options.D: Keep the narrative review format and add a second Claude pass that converts it into structured JSON findings

explanation: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` enforces structured output at the CLI level, guaranteeing well-formed JSON with the required fields (file path, line number, severity, suggested fix) that can be reliably parsed and posted as inline PR comments via the GitHub API. It uses built-in CLI capabilities designed specifically for structured output, rather than hoping the model formats correctly.

distractors.A: CLAUDE.md examples are probabilistic guidance; the model can still deviate, and any deviation breaks automated parsing.
distractors.C: A prompt-level text template is also probabilistic and fragile — a single malformed line breaks the parser, with no enforcement mechanism behind it.
distractors.D: A second conversion pass adds cost and latency, and the lossy narrative-to-JSON conversion can drop or distort findings.

stem: You need to add Slack as a new notification channel. The existing codebase has clear, established patterns for email, SMS, and push channels. However, Slack's API offers fundamentally different integration approaches—incoming webhooks (simple, one-way), bot tokens (delivery confirmation and programmatic control), or Slack Apps (two-way events, requires workspace approval). Your task says "add Slack support" without specifying the integration method or requiring advanced features like delivery tracking. How should you approach this task in Claude Code?

options.A: Start in direct execution mode using incoming webhooks to match the existing one-way notification pattern.
options.B: Switch to planning mode to weigh the integration options and present a recommendation before implementing.
options.C: Start in direct execution mode, scaffolding a Slack channel class on the existing patterns and deferring the method choice.
options.D: Start in direct execution mode using a bot-token approach to ensure delivery confirmation is possible.

explanation: Slack integration has multiple valid approaches with significantly different architectural implications, and the requirements are ambiguous. Planning mode lets you safely evaluate the trade-offs among webhooks, bot tokens, and Slack Apps and align on an approach before committing to implementation.

distractors.A: Choosing webhooks by analogy to existing channels silently forecloses delivery tracking and two-way features without ever surfacing the decision to stakeholders.
distractors.C: Scaffolding before choosing an integration method bakes in assumptions—the class interface differs meaningfully between webhooks, bot tokens, and Slack Apps.
distractors.D: Defaulting to bot tokens assumes a requirement (delivery confirmation) that was never stated, adding complexity that may be unnecessary.

stem: Your CLAUDE.md file has grown to 400+ lines containing coding standards, testing conventions, a detailed PR review checklist, deployment instructions, and database migration procedures. You want Claude to always follow the coding standards and testing conventions, but apply the PR review, deployment, and migration guidance only when actually doing those tasks. Which restructuring approach is most effective?

options.A: Move all guidance into separate skill files organized by workflow type, leaving only a brief project description in CLAUDE.md.
options.B: Keep everything in CLAUDE.md but use `@import` syntax to organize the content into separately maintained files by category.
options.C: Split CLAUDE.md into files under `.claude/rules/` with path-bound glob patterns so each rule loads only for the relevant file types.
options.D: Keep the universal standards in CLAUDE.md and move the workflow-specific guidance into skills with trigger keywords.

explanation: CLAUDE.md content loads in every session, which is exactly right for coding standards and testing conventions that must always apply. Skills are invoked on demand when Claude detects relevant triggers—ideal for workflow-specific guidance like PR review, deployment, and migrations that would otherwise waste always-on context.

distractors.A: Moving the universal standards into skills means they no longer load automatically in every session, so coding and testing conventions would only apply when a skill happens to be invoked.
distractors.B: `@import` improves maintainability but everything imported still loads into every session, so the workflow-specific content keeps consuming context on unrelated tasks.
distractors.C: Path-bound rules activate by file path, but PR review, deployment, and migrations are workflows, not file types—glob patterns are the wrong activation trigger for them.

stem: You're tasked with restructuring your team's monolithic application into microservices. The work impacts dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which Claude Code approach should you choose?

options.A: Switch to planning mode to explore the codebase and design the implementation approach before making changes.
options.B: Start in direct execution mode and switch to planning only after encountering unexpected complexity during implementation.
options.C: Start in direct execution mode and make incremental changes, letting the implementation reveal natural service boundaries.
options.D: Use direct execution mode with detailed upfront instructions that specify the structure of each service.

explanation: Planning mode is the right strategy for complex architectural restructuring like splitting a monolith: it allows safe, read-only exploration and informed decisions about service boundaries before committing to expensive changes across dozens of files.

distractors.B: Reactive planning after complexity bites means early changes were made without understanding dependencies, likely requiring rework of already-modified files.
distractors.C: Letting implementation reveal boundaries inverts the process—service boundaries are exactly the kind of cross-cutting decision that must be designed before code moves.
distractors.D: Detailed upfront instructions in execution mode assume you already know the right structure; without exploration, those instructions encode guesses about dependencies.

stem: Your team has used Claude Code for months. Recently, three developers report that Claude follows the guidance "always include comprehensive error handling," but a fourth developer who just joined says Claude does not follow it. All four work in the same repo and have up-to-date code. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.A: The guidance lives only in the original developers' user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`; move it to the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
options.B: The new developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` holds conflicting instructions that override the project settings; delete that section.
options.C: Claude Code learns per-user preferences over time, so the new developer must repeat the requirement until Claude "remembers" it.
options.D: Claude Code caches CLAUDE.md after the first read, so the others are running stale copies; everyone should clear the cache.

explanation: (A) is the simplest hypothesis that fits every fact in the stem: same repo, up-to-date code, and a split exactly along who has been on the team a while. Guidance added only to the original developers' user-level configs never reaches a new joiner. Moving it into the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is version-controlled and loaded for everyone, fixes it for all current and future members.

distractors.B: Possible, but a weaker first hypothesis: a brand-new joiner has a near-empty user config, and nothing in the stem suggests they authored a contradicting rule.
distractors.C: Claude Code does not accumulate per-user preferences over time. Persistent guidance comes from memory files, not repetition.
distractors.D: Memory files are read at session start rather than served from a long-lived cache, so cache-clearing is not the documented remedy and would not explain the split by tenure.

stem: You find that including 2–3 full endpoint implementation examples as context significantly improves consistency when generating new API endpoints. However, this context is useful only when creating new endpoints—not when debugging, reviewing code, or doing other work in the API directory. Which configuration approach is most effective?

options.A: Add the endpoint examples and pattern documentation to the project CLAUDE.md so they are always available.
options.B: Manually reference the endpoint examples in every generation request by copying the code into the prompt.
options.C: Configure path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/api/` that include the endpoint examples and activate in the API directory.
options.D: Create a skill that references the endpoint examples and carries the pattern-following instructions, invoked via a slash command.

explanation: A skill invoked on demand loads the bulky example context only for the task that needs it—generating new endpoints—and not during debugging, review, or other API-directory work. This keeps the main context clean while preserving high-quality, pattern-consistent generation when invoked.

distractors.A: CLAUDE.md content loads in every session, so several full endpoint implementations would permanently consume context even for tasks that never need them.
distractors.B: Manual copy-paste works but is error-prone and unscalable—every developer must remember to do it, and versions of the examples drift.
distractors.C: Path-bound rules activate for ANY work in the API directory, including debugging and review where the examples are explicitly not wanted; the trigger is task type, not file path.

stem: Your team created a `/migration` skill that generates database migration files, taking the migration name via `$ARGUMENTS`. In production you observe three issues: (1) developers often run the skill without arguments, causing poorly named files, (2) the skill sometimes uses database schema details from unrelated prior conversations, and (3) a developer accidentally ran destructive test cleanup because the skill had broad tool access. Which configuration approach fixes all three problems?

options.A: Use `$1` and `$2` instead of `$ARGUMENTS`, pull in schema files with `@` references, and warn about destructive operations in the description.
options.B: Add `argument-hint` to prompt for the required parameter, `context: fork` to isolate execution, and `allowed-tools` limited to file writes.
options.C: Split the skill into `/migration-create` and `/migration-apply`, request the name when it is missing, and scope `allowed-tools` for each.
options.D: Add SKILL.md instructions that validate `$ARGUMENTS`, tell the model to ignore prior conversation context, and list prohibited operations.

explanation: Each problem maps to a dedicated configuration feature: `argument-hint` surfaces the expected parameter at invocation time, reducing missing-argument runs; `context: fork` isolates execution so stale schema details from prior conversation cannot leak in; and `allowed-tools` deterministically constrains the skill to safe file-writing operations, preventing destructive actions.

distractors.A: Positional parameters do not stop developers from omitting arguments, `@` references add context but do not exclude polluted conversation history, and a frontmatter warning is advisory—nothing deterministically blocks destructive tool use.
distractors.C: Splitting the skill restructures the workflow but argument omission, context leakage, and tool scoping must still be solved within each new skill—the split itself fixes nothing.
distractors.D: All three fixes here are prompt-level instructions the model may not follow; instructions to 'ignore prior context' and 'avoid prohibited operations' are probabilistic, unlike fork isolation and tool restriction.

stem: You have a personal `/scratch` command that spins up throwaway analysis notes the way you like them. You want it available in every repository you work in, without committing it to any project or exposing it to teammates. Where should the command file live?

options.A: As a Markdown file under `~/.claude/commands/` in your home directory.
options.B: In `.claude/commands/` in each project repository, with the file added to `.gitignore`.
options.C: In a personal section at the bottom of each project's committed `CLAUDE.md`.
options.D: In `.claude/settings.local.json`, as an entry in a `commands` array.

explanation: User-level commands in `~/.claude/commands/` load in every project you open and live outside any repository, so they are never committed and never visible to teammates. This is the personal counterpart to project-level `.claude/commands/`, which is version-controlled and shared.

distractors.B: This works only if you recreate the file in every repo and keep the gitignore entry correct in each one; a single user-level file achieves the same thing everywhere with no per-repo maintenance.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md carries persistent instructions and context; it is not a mechanism for defining slash commands.
distractors.D: settings.local.json holds machine-local settings such as permissions. Slash commands are Markdown files in a commands directory, not entries in a settings array.

stem: Your team's CLAUDE.md grew beyond 500 lines, mixing TypeScript conventions, testing guidance, API patterns, and deployment procedures. Developers find it hard to locate and update the right sections. What approach does Claude Code support for organizing project-level instructions into focused topical modules?

options.A: Define a `.claude/config.yaml` mapping file patterns to specific sections inside CLAUDE.md.
options.B: Create separate Markdown files in `.claude/rules/`, each covering one topic (e.g., `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`).
options.C: Split the instructions into README.md files in relevant subdirectories that Claude automatically loads as instructions.
options.D: Create multiple files named CLAUDE.md at different levels of the directory tree, each overriding its parent's instructions.

explanation: Claude Code supports a `.claude/rules/` directory where teams create separate Markdown files for topical guidance (e.g., `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`), turning one unwieldy CLAUDE.md into focused, independently maintainable modules.

distractors.A: There is no `.claude/config.yaml` mechanism that maps file patterns to CLAUDE.md sections.
distractors.C: README.md files are ordinary documentation; Claude Code does not automatically load them as instruction memory.
distractors.D: Nested CLAUDE.md files add directory-scoped context but they do not override parent instructions, and scattering overrides is not the supported modularization pattern for topical organization.

stem: You are applying a large but mechanical change — renaming a function across about 30 files — and Claude Code prompts you to approve every individual file edit, which is slowing you down. You still want to manually review any shell commands Claude wants to run. Which permission mode best fits?

options.A: bypassPermissions — skip all permission prompts for the session, including shell commands
options.B: plan mode — Claude proposes the full set of edits but does not apply any of them
options.C: default — keep approving each individual file edit as it is proposed
options.D: acceptEdits — auto-approve file edits for the session, still prompting for other actions

explanation: (D) acceptEdits automatically accepts file-edit tool calls for the session, removing the per-edit prompts on a trusted, well-scoped mechanical change, while still prompting for higher-risk actions such as Bash commands. That is exactly the requirement: fast edits, but keep a gate on shell commands.

distractors.A: bypassPermissions removes every prompt, shell commands included, which breaks the stated requirement to keep reviewing them; it belongs only in fully sandboxed environments.
distractors.B: plan mode is read-only, so Claude would propose all 30 edits and apply none of them — the rename never lands.
distractors.C: default is the mode the developer is already in, so it changes nothing about the per-edit prompting they are trying to eliminate.

stem: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively to run the test suite and the linter, and you want a least-privilege setup that deterministically limits which shell commands it can execute without a human approving each one. Select the TWO mechanisms that restrict which commands Claude Code may run without prompting.

options.A: A permissions.allow allowlist in .claude/settings.json naming exact tool patterns like Bash(npm run test:*)
options.B: A permissions.deny list in .claude/settings.json blocking specific dangerous commands, e.g. Bash(rm:*)
options.C: A note in CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to run only the project's test and lint commands and nothing else
options.D: Running the job in bypassPermissions mode so the non-interactive pipeline never blocks on a prompt

explanation: settings.json permission rules are the deterministic controls. An allow allowlist grants only the enumerated tool patterns to run without prompting, and a deny list unconditionally blocks specific dangerous commands. Used together they implement least-privilege tool access for an automated, non-interactive run.

distractors.C: A CLAUDE.md instruction is probabilistic guidance the model may not follow; it does not deterministically restrict which commands can execute.
distractors.D: bypassPermissions removes all permission checks — the opposite of least privilege — allowing any command to run without prompting.

stem: Your organization publishes an enterprise-managed policy that denies Bash(curl:*) for all Claude Code users. A project's committed .claude/settings.json lists Bash(curl:*) in its allow rules, and one developer also adds it to their personal .claude/settings.local.json. When that developer runs Claude Code in the project and Claude tries to run curl, what happens?

options.A: curl runs, because the developer's settings.local.json allow rule is the most specific and wins
options.B: curl runs, because the project's committed .claude/settings.json allow rule grants it to the team
options.C: curl is denied, because enterprise-managed policy sits at the top of the precedence chain
options.D: Claude prompts the developer, because the conflicting allow and deny rules cancel each other out

explanation: Settings precedence runs enterprise-managed policy above all project and user settings, including both the shared .claude/settings.json and the personal .claude/settings.local.json. An enterprise deny rule is authoritative and cannot be overridden by a project or personal allow rule, so curl is denied.

distractors.A: settings.local.json overrides the shared .claude/settings.json, but neither overrides enterprise-managed policy; specificity does not trump the hierarchy.
distractors.B: A committed project allow rule grants a tool only in the absence of a higher-precedence deny; the enterprise-managed deny sits above it and wins.
distractors.D: Rules do not cancel out; the highest-precedence rule (the enterprise deny) governs deterministically rather than falling back to a prompt.

stem: A unit test fails with a stack trace pointing to a single off-by-one error in one utility function. The cause is clear and the fix is confined to that one function. Which Claude Code approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Enter plan mode first so Claude explores the codebase and presents a plan before touching anything
options.B: Execute the fix directly in the single utility function the stack trace points to
options.C: Restructure the surrounding module in plan mode to prevent similar bugs in the future
options.D: Delegate the fix to a separate reviewer subagent before making any change to the function

explanation: (B) is the least intervention that treats the diagnosed cause. The stack trace already pinpoints a single off-by-one in one function, so the change is well-scoped and mechanical — direct execution is appropriate. Plan mode exists for large, multi-file, or architecturally ambiguous work; adding it (or an extra reviewer subagent) here is pure overhead.

distractors.A: Whole-codebase exploration is overhead the stem has already made unnecessary: the cause is known and the scope is one function.
distractors.C: Restructuring the module is scope creep well beyond the reported bug, and it risks new defects in code that currently works.
distractors.D: An independent reviewer pays off on ambiguous or high-risk changes; on a one-line correction with a stack trace pointing at it, it is process for its own sake.

stem: You ask Claude to "reformat these API responses into our standard shape," but across runs it interprets "standard shape" inconsistently — sometimes nesting, sometimes flattening, sometimes renaming fields differently. The prose description clearly is not pinning it down. What most reliably fixes this?

options.A: Provide 2-3 concrete input->output examples of a raw response mapped to the standard shape
options.B: Add emphatic words like "carefully" and "exactly" to the instruction and re-run it
options.C: Lower the temperature so the transformation comes out deterministic across runs
options.D: Ask Claude to first explain what it thinks "standard shape" means before transforming

explanation: When a natural-language description is interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate the exact transformation — a few worked examples pin down nesting, naming, and structure far better than more adjectives or a temperature change.

distractors.B: Emphatic adjectives do not remove the ambiguity in "standard shape"; the model still guesses at the mapping.
distractors.C: Temperature reduces randomness but not the underlying ambiguity — a deterministic wrong interpretation is still wrong.
distractors.D: Having it explain its interpretation surfaces the ambiguity but does not resolve it; you still have not shown the target shape.

stem: You are using Claude Code to implement a tricky date-rollover utility and want it to converge on correct behavior including edge cases (leap years, month boundaries, DST) rather than iterating vaguely. What is the most effective way to drive the iteration?

options.A: Describe all the edge cases in prose in one large prompt and ask for a complete implementation
options.B: Ask Claude to implement the utility, then manually eyeball the output for edge-case bugs
options.C: Raise the thinking budget so Claude reasons longer about the edge cases before writing code
options.D: Write the edge-case test suite first, have Claude implement against it, and feed back the failing tests

explanation: Test-driven iteration — write tests (including edge cases) first, implement against them, then iterate by sharing the specific failures — gives concrete, objective feedback that guides the model toward correctness far more reliably than prose descriptions or manual inspection.

distractors.A: A single prose description of edge cases is easy to under-specify, and you get no objective signal about what is still wrong.
distractors.B: Eyeballing output is error-prone and gives no systematic coverage of the edge cases.
distractors.C: More thinking time helps reasoning but provides no concrete pass/fail signal to iterate against; it does not replace tests.

stem: You ask Claude to add caching to an unfamiliar service. There are decisions it cannot safely assume (invalidation strategy, cache-key scope, failure behavior), and you want to avoid it charging ahead on wrong assumptions. What is the best approach, including how to batch interacting vs independent fixes?

options.A: Tell it to make reasonable assumptions and proceed, then fix whatever turns out to be wrong afterwards
options.B: Use the interview pattern to surface the decisions first, then batch interacting fixes and sequence independent ones
options.C: Write one giant prompt containing every detail you can think of so no clarifying questions are needed
options.D: Have it implement three separate caching designs in parallel and pick whichever one looks best

explanation: (B) is right on both halves of the question. The interview pattern has Claude ask clarifying questions to surface the decisions it cannot safely assume — invalidation strategy, cache-key scope, failure behaviour — before writing code in an unfamiliar service. On batching: interacting problems should be fixed together in one message so the model can see how they constrain each other, while independent problems can be handed over sequentially.

distractors.A: Assume-and-fix invites rework on decisions that were knowable up front, and in an unfamiliar service the wrong invalidation strategy is expensive to unwind.
distractors.C: A giant up-front prompt still cannot anticipate what the model actually needs clarified — you are guessing at the questions instead of letting it ask them.
distractors.D: Three parallel implementations spend the effort before the decisions are settled; the cheap step is asking, not building.
